title: Fantasia
oneLine: An autonomous agent that researches, builds and ships one AI project a night. 50 shipped in 54 nights for $7.35 in metered API cost, inside a sandbox I designed.

specs.Role: Solo: the pipeline, the evaluation stages and the sandbox. The agents built the nightly projects.
specs.Hardware: Mac Mini M4, 16 GB, headless, always on, at home
specs.Models: Grok for the scout, Claude for pick, plan and review, Codex for the build
specs.Stack: Claude Code, Codex, Python, Bash, launchd, tmux, GitHub CLI, Tailscale, Cloudflare
specs.Output: 50 public repos under the agent's own GitHub account, each live on its own subdomain

intro: Artax is a Mac Mini in my house that runs AI coding agents unattended. Every night a pipeline I built scouts X for the day's most interesting AI work, picks one idea, plans it, builds it, tests it in a headless browser, publishes it to its own subdomain and public GitHub repo, and then reviews its own work. Nobody is awake while this happens.

I built the system. The agents built the 50 projects. The pipeline also failed on 4 nights, and it publishes those nights with its reasoning. The agent runs with permission prompts switched off, so the other half of the project is the containment around it.
On the names: Artax is the machine and the agent, and fantasia.build is where it publishes. Both are borrowed from The Neverending Story.

sections.label: Pipeline
sections.title: How a night works
body: A night is seven stages. Three different models do the work, and two of the stages are plain local code with no model at all. The timings below are from the 12 November 2026 run.
Two components run on the box. Hermes is the runtime, which I can also reach over Telegram. Auryn is the nightly builder. Both repos are private for now.

flow.summary: Seven stages run in order each night: scout with Grok, pick with Claude, plan with Claude, build with Codex, a local deterministic gate, a local publish step, and a review by Claude in a fresh context. A plan that cannot be built honestly is recorded as blocked, a failed gate means nothing ships, and the review can propose changes to the pipeline itself.

boxes.title: Scout
boxes.note: Grok, X search. 50.9s. Returns the night's candidate ideas with source links.

stages.label: candidates

boxes.title: Pick
boxes.note: Claude. 68.4s. Scores each candidate from 1 to 5 on surprise, demonstrability, self-containedness and honesty.

stages.aside: It writes down why it turned the others away.

stages.label: one idea

boxes.title: Plan
boxes.note: Claude. 68.4s. Writes the approach and the acceptance criteria as checkable assertions.

stages.aside: Cannot be built honestly within the constraints? The night is recorded as blocked.

boxes.title: Build
boxes.note: Codex. 212.4s. Implements the plan inside the sandboxed account.

stages.label: project directory

boxes.title: Gate
boxes.note: Local, deterministic. 3.1s. Output exists, assets resolve, the page loads in a headless browser with no console errors.

stages.aside: A failed gate means nothing ships.

boxes.note: Local. 14.1s. Pushes a public repo and deploys to Cloudflare.

boxes.title: Review
boxes.note: Claude, fresh context. 139.9s. Grades the shipped artifact on shipped, honest, worth it and efficient.

stages.aside: Can propose changes to the pipeline's own build prompt and model routing when a problem keeps recurring.

sections.label: Evaluation
sections.title: It does not trust its own output
body: A pipeline that ships whatever the model produces is a demo. What separates this from one is the places where the system checks itself. There are five.

Before the build, the pick stage scores every candidate against a fixed rubric and records why it rejected the rest. The plan stage then writes the acceptance criteria before any code exists, as assertions that can be checked. Two examples: "the seed table has at least 15 rows on load" and "no network request leaves the page's own origin".
After the build, the gate is deterministic code, not a model's opinion. If it fails, nothing ships. Then a separate reviewer, started in a fresh context, grades what was actually published.

The last check is that failures are published. Every night has a public page, whether it shipped or not. A shipped night shows its scores, its rejected candidates and its gate results. A failed night shows why it stopped.

images.alt: The pick scoring for the 12 November night: surprise 4, demonstrability 4, self-containedness 5, honesty 4, followed by a paragraph explaining why this idea was chosen over the other candidates
images.caption: Before the build: rubric scores and the written reasoning

images.alt: The review scoring for the same night: shipped 5, honest 5, worth it 4, efficient 5, mean 4.75 out of 5, followed by a note that no change to the build prompt or routing was needed
images.caption: After the build: the reviewer's grades for the same night

after: The average self-review score is 4.08 out of 5 as of 13 November 2026. That is the pipeline grading itself. It is not a human rating.
The reviewer does mark things down. Token Diet, a BPE tokenizer comparison, shipped and passed the gate and still got 2.8.

sections.label: Failure
sections.title: The night it refused to ship
body: On 11 October the pick was a storefront with a live AI sales agent. The plan stage worked out that a real live chat needs either an API key exposed in client-side code or a backend, and both are outside its constraints. The only static version would be a scripted decision tree pretending to be an agent.
It recorded the night as failed and published the reasoning. That is the behaviour I wanted: a blocked night is a better result than a mock-up that claims to be something it is not.

images.alt: The public page for the failed night, titled Storefront Clerk with a red Failed badge and the date 2026-10-11. Under the heading Approach, a paragraph explains that a live chat needs either a key shipped in client-side code or a backend, that a canned decision tree would be a page that pretends, and that the night is recorded as blocked rather than shipped as a mockup.
images.caption: The published reasoning for the failed night of 11 October 2026

sections.label: Containment
sections.title: Permissions off, operating system on
body: The agent runs with permission prompts off, using --dangerously-skip-permissions. An unattended machine cannot stop and ask. So the boundaries are operating system, git and network boundaries.
The design assumption behind all of it: the agent's home directory can be destroyed at any moment, and anything that matters is already on GitHub.
sections.callout: The flag removes the prompts. The operating system remains.

images.alt: A page from the runbook I wrote, headed "Four cheap layers, and one that isn't". A table lists five layers and what each stops: separate machine, non-admin macOS user, separate GitHub identity, no access to your repos, and network reach, which is marked as not solved by default. A note below says to assume the agent's home directory can be destroyed at any moment.
images.caption: The sandbox layers, from the runbook I wrote for the machine

facts.Machine: A separate Mac Mini, not my laptop.
facts.Account: artax, a standard macOS user with no sudo. My own home directory on the box is mode 700, because macOS ships home directories readable by every local user.
facts.GitHub identity: artaxlives, created 17 September 2026, with its own SSH key generated on the box. It has no collaborator access to any of my repos. It ships into repos it owns, or forks and opens a pull request.
facts.Network: A Tailscale policy with two grants: my devices can reach each other, and my devices can reach the box on TCP 22. The box's tag is never a source, so it cannot open a connection to my laptop or phone.
facts.Hooks: guard.py runs before every shell command. A global git pre-push hook refuses pushes to protected branches on any repo that is not the bot's own.
facts.Kill switch: Revoke one SSH key and one token.

after: The limits are part of the design, so I state them. The regex hook is a backstop against accidents. The non-admin account is the real boundary. The home LAN outside Tailscale is still reachable from the box, and that is a known open gap.

sections.label: Guard hook
sections.title: What the hook allows and refuses
body: guard.py is a 91-line Python hook with no dependencies. It runs before every shell command the agent issues. This is its real output on 13 commands: 4 allowed, 9 refused.

It allows rm -rf node_modules on purpose. A guard rail that blocks normal work teaches an agent to route around it. The last two git rows are the two ways of disabling the pre-push hook, and the shell hook blocks both.

sections.label: Lessons
sections.title: What running it taught me
body: A blanket "never push to main" rule once stranded a correct self-repair on a branch nothing ran. I narrowed the rule so it protects my repos and lets the bot own its trunk.
GitHub's free tier does not protect branches on private repos, so the local hook is the only enforcement there.
On Apple Silicon a FileVault-locked Mac can be unlocked over SSH after a power cut, but only over Ethernet.
Scraped posts and web pages are untrusted input to an agent that can run code. The next version separates a tool-less research step that produces structured briefs from the builder that reads them.
